meta.title_plain: How prime numbers guard your secrets
meta.teaser: Prime numbers are easy to multiply but hard to split, and that protects your accounts.

page.title: How prime numbers guard your secrets
page.bigIdea: Multiplying two big prime numbers is easy. Splitting the answer back apart is so hard it keeps your messages safe.

cards.title: The rectangle test
cards.front: Why can't 7 bricks make a rectangle?
cards.back: A prime is a number above 1 that only divides by 1 and itself. Twelve bricks make a 3 by 4 rectangle. Seven bricks only make one long line.
cards.tryit: Take 12 LEGO bricks and find every rectangle you can make. Now try 13 bricks. What happens?

cards.title: Maths' building blocks
cards.front: Every number hides a recipe made of primes.
cards.back: Every number above 1 is made by multiplying primes, in exactly one way. For example, 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Primes are the bricks of numbers.
cards.tryit: Break 84 into primes. Start by halving it, and keep going until every piece is prime.

cards.title: A one-way street
cards.front: Easy one way, super hard the other way.
cards.back: Multiplying two huge primes takes a computer a blink. Going backwards, from the answer to the two primes, is so hard that nobody knows a fast way.
cards.tryit: Time yourself working out 13 × 17. Then time how long it takes to split 143 into two primes.

cards.title: A lock anyone can see
cards.front: How can a lock be public but still safe?
cards.back: In 1977, three MIT scientists built RSA. Your public key is two secret primes multiplied. Anyone can lock a message with it. Only the primes unlock it.
cards.tryit: Next time you see a padlock icon in your browser, remember: maths like this is working behind it.

cards.title: Your challenge
cards.front: 391 is two primes multiplied together. Can you crack the code and find them?
cards.back: 391 = 17 × 23. Since 20 × 20 = 400, one prime must be below 20. Test 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, then 17 works!
cards.tryit: Ask Dad to multiply two primes under 30 in secret. Crack his number with pencil and paper.

words.d: A number above 1 that only divides evenly by 1 and itself.
A number above 1 that can be split into smaller factors.
A number that divides into another number with nothing left over.
The answer you get when you multiply numbers together.
Scrambling a message so only the right person can read it.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is prime?
quiz.hint: Add up the digits. If the total divides by 3, so does the number.
quiz.why: 51 = 3 × 17 and 57 = 3 × 19, but nothing splits 53 except 1 and 53.

quiz.q: Euclid's trick: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 210. What happens when you divide 211 by 2, 3, 5 or 7?
quiz.hint: 210 divides evenly by all four. What does adding 1 do to the remainder?
quiz.why: Each one fits into 210 exactly, so 211 always leaves 1 over, which is how Euclid showed primes never run out.

quiz.q: How many prime numbers are there from 1 to 20?
quiz.hint: Write 1 to 20, cross out 1, then cross out multiples of 2 and 3 (but not 2 and 3 themselves).
quiz.why: The primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19, which makes eight.

quiz.q: In RSA, what is the public key made from?
quiz.hint: Think about the one-way street: which job is easy and which is hard?
quiz.why: Multiplying is easy, but splitting the product back into its primes is very hard, so the primes stay secret.

page.think: Imagine you and a friend invent a secret code for messages in Roblox. What would make it easy for you to use, but hard for anyone else to crack?
